nameStory: The name 'Lady's-mantle' comes from the shape of the leaves, which supposedly resemble a lady's cloak or mantle spread out. The 'thin-stem' part of this species' name refers to its notably slender stems, which help distinguish it from its stouter relatives.
description: Thin-stem Lady's-mantle is a small perennial herb in the rose family, though you'd never guess it's related to roses at first glance! This delicate plant produces tiny, inconspicuous greenish flowers and distinctive rounded leaves. It's a low-growing species that forms small patches, rarely getting more than a few inches tall.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Rounded to kidney-shaped leaves with shallow lobes around the edges, like a fan or tiny cape. The leaves feel soft and may collect dewdrops in their center, creating a silvery appearance in morning light.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellow-green flowers without petals, clustered in small groups. Each flower is only about 1/8 inch across and easy to overlook - they look more like little green specks than typical flowers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low mats or small clumps close to the ground. The entire plant typically stays under 6 inches tall, with a delicate, almost fragile appearance.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Notably thin and wiry stems that feel almost thread-like when you gently touch them. Much more slender than other Lady's-mantles you might encounter.

habitat: Thin-stem Lady's-mantle is extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation in the region. When found, it typically grows in disturbed soils, along pathways, or in areas with poor, gravelly ground where other plants struggle to establish.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as small, folded fans that gradually open and spread. Early flowers may begin appearing in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time with tiny greenish blooms. Leaves are fully developed and at their most recognizable, often holding morning dew beautifully.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back. Seeds are ripening and dispersing during this time.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground parts. No above-ground features visible for identification.

funFact: Lady's-mantles were once believed by medieval alchemists to have magical properties because of the way their leaves collect and hold perfect spheres of dewdrops - they thought this 'celestial water' could turn base metals into gold!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other Lady's-mantles, but the thin, wiry stems are the giveaway. Garden Lady's-mantle has much thicker, more robust stems and larger leaves, while this species looks delicate and almost wispy in comparison.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the rose family, Lady's-mantles look nothing like roses - they lack the showy petals and thorns we associate with their famous relatives. The family connection becomes clearer when you examine the flower structure closely under a magnifying glass.
compareHints: Thin-stem Lady's-mantle is distinguished from Garden Lady's-mantle by its much more delicate build and notably slender stems. Unlike the robust Garden Lady's-mantle commonly grown in flower borders, this species has a fragile, almost ephemeral quality that makes it easy to overlook entirely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Garden lady's-mantle is much larger and more robust than its relatives like slender parsley-piert, which has tiny divided leaves and grows as a small annual weed.
Slender parsley-piert differs dramatically from its showy cousin Garden Lady's-mantle, which has large, soft leaves and grows over a foot tall.
Velvet Lady's-mantle is distinguished from other Lady's-mantles by its exceptionally hairy, truly velvety texture throughout.
